implementation_notes: C++20 gives std::atomic<T>::wait and notify_one/notify_all, which turn the spin-wait on head/tail into a blocking wait - useful when the ring is the generalisation of a blocking bounded queue. But the high-performance answer is a hand-written SPSC ring with std::atomic indices (acquire/release) and no virtual dispatch, often using a power-of-two mask and alignas on the indices. boost::circular_buffer is the general-purpose library version (dynamic, thread-safe with an optional locking policy, with iterator invalidation documented) and is the right choice when the ring must be resizable or when arbitrary iteration is needed; the hand-written one is for a fixed-size, allocation-free, real-time path. Note that std::atomic's wait requires a value-change notification, so a naive index-wait ring can miss a transition - the classic lost-wakeup in a ring-based queue.
idiom_name: hand-written SPSC ring with std::atomic indices (or boost::circular_buffer for the general dynamic case)
pitfalls: head - tail == N as the full test assumes indices wrap only modulo N; with a power-of-two mask and monotonic counters this is correct, but a reader who masks head itself will break it.
The head must be published with release AFTER the item write, and the tail must be acquired BEFORE the item read - reversing either is the classic bug.
alignas(64) on each index: they are written by different cores every operation and sharing a line makes the lock-free ring slower than a mutex.
std::atomic::wait can lose a notification if the value changed between the load and the wait - a fixed-size ring is usually simpler without wait/notify than with it.
boost::circular_buffer invalidates iterators on resize and its thread-safety is opt-in via a locking policy - read the docs before using it as a drop-in.
